questions.explanation: The key O(1) area mechanism is incremental maintenance using the shoelace formula. Rather than recalculating area from all h vertices each query, store area as a running sum. When merging a batch, new hull vertices are inserted between existing ones; each insertion adds the cross-product of the triangle formed by (previous_vertex, new_vertex, next_vertex), computed as (prev.x*new.y + new.x*next.y + next.x*prev.y - prev.y*new.x - new.y*next.x - next.y*prev.x)/2. This is O(1) per new vertex. Since vertices are only added (never removed in this batch model), area monotonically increases and queries return the cached value in O(1). The merge operation achieves O(B + h) by exploiting monotonicity: sorted batch points are merged with sorted chain vertices in a linear sweep, with stack operations for convexity maintenance. Binary search for point-in-hull works by finding where the query point's x-coordinate would fit in the chain's x-sequence, then testing orientation against the supporting edge—standard O(log h) algorithm for convex polygons. Rebuilding is O(n log n) per batch, making incremental updates asymptotically superior for small B relative to n.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design streaming data structures with strong amortized bounds and to reason about substring counts.

## Key Concepts
- Suffix Automaton, online extension by characters, cloning, amortized analysis, distinct substrings.
- Complexity: per-character O(1) amortized; memory O(n).
- Batch processing implications for streaming inputs.

## Code Example
```cpp
struct SAMState { int link, len; int next[ALPH]; SAMState(){link=-1;len=0; memset(next,-1,sizeof(next));} };
vector<SAMState> st(1);
int last=0; long long total=0;
void sam_extend(int c){ int cur=st.size(); st.push_back(SAMState()); st[cur].len=st[last].len+1; int p=last; while(p!=-1 && st[p].next[c]==-1){ st[p].next[c]=cur; p=st[p].link; } if(p==-1){ st[cur].link=0; } else { int q=st[p].next[c]; if(st[p].len+1==st[q].len){ st[cur].link=q; } else { int clone=st.size(); st.push_back(st[q]); st[clone].len=st[p].len+1; while(p!=-1 && st[p].next[c]==q){ st[p].next[c]=clone; p=st[p].link; } st[q].link=st[cur].link=clone; } } last=cur; total += st[cur].len - st[st[cur].link].len; }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would deletions or edits affect the approach?
- How to scale with large alphabets and memory constraints?

This question assesses practical knowledge of streaming algorithms for frequency analysis—a core skill for systems handling high-volume data streams. It evaluates understanding of the space-accuracy trade-off fundamental to approximate algorithms.

- **Top-K**: Returning the K most frequent elements with approximate counts
- **Batch processing**: Handling grouped updates efficiently
- **Error guarantees**: Bounded recall but possible false positives
